title: Short Stuff: What is Latinx anyway?
summary: Short Stuff episode on the term "Latinx" (also written Latin X or latin x). Josh and Chuck discuss how racial and ethnic labels shift over time and by region, using the history of "Chicano" (a term of derision that became one of pride during the Mexican student movement in California and the farm workers movement) and the parallel with "black." They cover "Hispanic" as the U.S. Census Bureau's longstanding term, its falling favor, and historian Paul Ortiz's views (University of Florida), including that Hispanic was embraced in Florida but resented in California and Washington. The hosts explain Latinx as a gender-neutral, inclusive "bridge-building" term, note that Latino is often associated with Mexican origin, and cite a Pew survey finding that only about three percent of Hispanics use the term, while most have heard of it. They discuss alternatives such as Latina with an accent mark, and close by reminding listeners that people within any group disagree and that one should let individuals state their own identity.

segments.title: Why a new term for the Latino community
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of a new term for the Latino community, noting that people decide what they want to be called and that terms shift in fashion, offense and geography. They frame racial groups as social and cultural constructs with many internal differences.

segments.title: Chicano and reclaiming a derogatory term
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Chicano, which was a term of derision before being adopted as a term of pride during the Mexican student movement in California and the farm workers movement. Paul Ortiz, a University of Florida professor, compares this to the reclaiming of the word black during the Civil Rights movement.

segments.title: Hispanic and the U.S. Census Bureau
segments.summary: Hispanic was the common term for a long time and is the Census Bureau's longstanding term, though its definition is a jumble. Ortiz said Hispanic was resented as a government label in California and Washington but embraced in Florida, showing that preference depends on place.

segments.title: Break and mystery word setup
segments.summary: A break in which the hosts tease the mystery term and joke about a masked singing show.

segments.title: Pronouncing Latinx and its purpose
segments.summary: The hosts explain the pronunciations Latin X, latin x and Latinx, and describe the term as a gender-neutral, inclusive umbrella for people who identify as Latino, Latina, Hispanic or Chicano. Surveys show most people prefer their nation of origin, but a younger, English-speaking group is adopting Latinx. Latino is often associated with Mexican origin, which leaves others out.

segments.title: Pew survey, alternatives and group disagreement
segments.summary: A Pew survey found most Hispanics have heard the term Latinx but only about three percent use it. The hosts note younger users are more vocal online. Alternatives like Latina with an accent mark are raised, and the hosts stress that people within any group disagree and should be allowed to name their own identity.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the episode and give production credits.
